idiom_name: ActiveRecord id column (bigint primary key by convention) / id: :uuid
implementation_notes: ActiveRecord supplies the identity field by convention: every table gets an integer column named id as the primary key (bigint on PostgreSQL/MySQL, integer on SQLite), migrations create it automatically, the model exposes it as #id, and new_record? distinguishes an unsaved instance (id nil) from a persisted one. The classic key-generator object is replaced by the column default plus the connection adapter; a UUID key is opted into per table (id: :uuid with gen_random_uuid()) or assigned in a before_create callback, and composite primary keys are declared explicitly where a link table genuinely needs them. Use the default integral key unless keys must be known before insert or generated across shards.
code_sketch:
class CreateOrders < ActiveRecord::Migration[8.1]
  def change
    create_table :orders do |t|   # id: bigint pk, created for you
      t.string :name
    end
  end
end

o = Order.create!(name: "A-1")
o.id           # set by the INSERT (RETURNING)
o.new_record?  # false
pitfalls: id is nil until the record is saved: use new_record? for the unsaved state instead of treating nil/0 as a real identity in caches or comparisons.
A UUID primary key must be chosen in the migration and the model from the start; retrofitting one later breaks every reference, URL and cached key.
Rails 7.1+ models with composite primary keys have no implicit single id, so code assuming find(id) or params[:id] must be updated for those tables.
